When the Annex A objectives are graded, evidence that is heuristic, untagged, or declared without a rostered signer is set aside as advisory before anything is counted. It is listed beside its objective but cannot make it satisfied, partial or failing. NoteThe MISRA rule engine's findings are tagged derived, but the rule engine's runs are not yet used as evidence for objectives: A-5 coding-standard evidence still comes from cppcheck. See MISRA rule engine.

clang must be installed; there is no bundled parser. Without the Arm GNU Toolchain's newlib headers, affected translation units are missing from the model. IAR @ placement and TI section pragmas are not modelled. C++ translation units (.cpp, .cc, .cxx, .C, -x c++ or a g++ / clang++ driver) are modelled with their functions and methods under qualified names (ns::Class::method), plus classes, bases, virtual members, namespaces, templates and using-directives. Templates are modelled as written, once, not per instantiation. Functions containing try/catch, throw or range-based for have no control-flow graph (cfg: null), and the model index lists this under its limitations. Building the model from the interrupt analysis shows no progress and cannot be cancelled. Progress is also not reported when the build runs on a single worker (3 cores or fewer, or NOYCE_MODEL_JOBS=1).

Noyce IDE checks MISRA C:2012 (including Amendments 1 to 4) with its own rule engine, which reads a clang-parsed model of the code rather than matching lines of text. It runs next to cppcheck, not instead of it: where the two disagree you see both, and nothing is merged. Open MISRA Diagnostics and select Scan; see Analysis & proof for the rest of the view.

The engine implements part of MISRA C:2012. It does not claim full compliance checking, and the count is not fixed in these docs: it is read from the guideline catalogue that ships with Noyce IDE (services/noyce-core/rules/misra-c-2012.json, one entry per guideline with implemented: true or false). The MISRA Diagnostics page subtitle shows the count for your last scan, for example "Guidelines checked: n of total (MISRA C:2012 rules and directives)", and "· n TUs not checked" when some translation units could not be checked. Before any scan it reads "Guidelines checked: Not measured (MISRA C:2012)". Both numbers count rules and directives. No guideline text is shipped; it is MISRA's copyright. If you hold a licence, put headline texts in .noyce/rules/headlines.json as {"Rule 10.4": "…"} and the Compliance Summary shows a Headline column. There is no import screen for this file. Some rules cannot always be decided from the code alone. For those the engine reports a possible violation with its reasoning instead of a violation.

Scan in MISRA Diagnostics runs cppcheck and the rule engine together. The rule engine shows "Rule engine: x/y TUs · file" while it runs, with Cancel rule scan. It times out after 120 seconds by default; the cppcheck budget setting in the view also sets the rule engine's time limit. A scan that times out or is cancelled reads "Not measured — timed out" or "Not measured — cancelled", never compliant. From a terminal, noyce analyze runs the same scan. Results are written to .noyce/analysis/rules/results.json. Code classified as vendor code (for example Drivers/, CMSIS/, HAL, Middlewares/, third_party/) is excluded automatically and reported separately under Excluded adopted code.

.noyce/rules.json sets which guidelines apply to your project. There is no editor for it in the IDE; write it by hand. Without the file, every implemented guideline is enabled: jsonCopy{ "schema": "noyce.rules-config/1", "edition": "MISRA C:2012", "enabled": ["*"], "disabled": ["Rule 15.5"], "recategorize": { "Rule 15.7": "required", "Rule 2.7": "disapplied" }, "exclude": ["src/generated/**"], "timeoutSeconds": 300 } Field Meaning schema, edition schema must be noyce.rules-config/1 and edition must start with MISRA C:2012 (the catalogue's longer edition name is accepted). Anything else discards the whole file and applies the defaults, with a "Rule configuration problems" notice. enabled, disabled Guideline ids such as "Rule 10.4", or "*". recategorize Per MISRA Compliance:2020: raise a guideline's category (advisory → required → mandatory), or set an advisory guideline to disapplied. Lowering a category is ignored with a notice. exclude Path globs relative to the project root. * does not cross /; ** does. timeoutSeconds The rule engine's time limit (1 to 1800). Unknown guideline ids and malformed fields are reported in the Compliance Summary under Rule configuration problems.

The Compliance Summary tab gives one row per guideline, in the style of MISRA Compliance:2020: Guideline, Kind, Category (with "re-categorised from …" where you changed it), Compliance, Violations, Possible and Deviations. Tiles and filters count Compliant, Compliant with deviations, Violations, Disapplied and Not checked. A guideline is: Disapplied if your rule set disapplies it; Not checked if it is not implemented, not enabled, or was not run; Violations if any violation or possible violation remains; Not checked if the scan was incomplete: a translation unit failed to parse or timed out. One file that fails to parse turns every guideline without findings into Not checked rather than Compliant; Compliant with deviations if every finding is covered by an approved deviation; Compliant otherwise.

A finding counts as compliant with deviation only when a deviation in Evidence Records → MISRA deviations covers it: same rule (or *), matching file and lines or vendor directory, status approved, with a rationale, an assessed risk, an approval date and an approver who is a person on the roster. A mandatory guideline cannot be deviated. WarningThe rule engine reads deviations from .noyce/process/deviations/ and the roster from .noyce/process/roster/ (one file per record, as the IDE saves them), plus anything still in the older single files. When a project keeps no roster at all, any approver who is not an AI agent is accepted.

The Disagreements tab compares the rule engine's findings with cppcheck's MISRA addon, for the rules both implement: Only Noyce rule engine, Only cppcheck, Agreed locations and Outside rule overlap, then a table of each disagreement. "Disagreements are reviewed, not merged." It needs a completed run of both.

C++ translation units are checked against MISRA C++:2023, and C translation units against MISRA C:2012: each rule set runs only on its own language, and one project can have both. A unit is C++ when its compile command selects C++ (-x c++, or a g++ / clang++ / c++ driver) or its file ends in .cpp, .cc, .cxx or .C. The C++ standard appears only when the last scan found at least one C++ unit. The engine implements a first slice of 31 of the 179 MISRA C++:2023 guidelines. All 31 are decidable rules whose construct is unambiguous in the clang AST: C-style, functional and reinterpret_cast casts, pointer/integer casts, null pointer constants other than nullptr, goto, unbraced bodies, else if chains, the comma operator, unary +, several variables in one declaration, asm, bit-fields, union, virtual inheritance, virtual / override / final, non-explicit converting constructors and conversion operators, overloaded && / || / unary &, pointer exception objects, throw; outside a handler, program-terminating functions, #pragma, atof-family functions, offsetof, <cstdarg> and std::vector<bool>. The catalogue is services/noyce-core/rules/misra-cpp-2023.json. The page subtitle adds "· n of 179 (MISRA C++:2023, m C++ TUs)" after the MISRA C count. C++ findings appear in the Findings tab with the rule shown as "MISRA C++:2023 Rule 9.6.1". The Compliance Summary tab gets a MISRA C:2012 / MISRA C++:2023 switch. The C++ summary uses the same compliance rules as MISRA C, over C++ units only. WarningThe guideline ids, categories, decidability and scope in the C++ catalogue come from one public listing (codeql-coding-standards rules.csv) and were not cross-checked against a second source. Every entry is marked review: "unconfirmed", and the C++ summary shows a "Guideline categories unconfirmed" notice. Confirm the categories against your licensed copy, and correct one with cpp.recategorize until then. To configure C++, add a cpp section to .noyce/rules.json beside the MISRA C settings: jsonCopy{ "schema": "noyce.rules-config/1", "edition": "MISRA C:2012", "disabled": ["Rule 15.5"], "exclude": ["src/generated/**"], "cpp": { "disabled": ["Rule 9.6.1"], "recategorize": { "Rule 8.2.2": "mandatory" } } } A C++-only project can put "edition": "MISRA C++:2023" at the top level instead; MISRA C then uses its defaults for any C units. The cpp section takes the same enabled, disabled, recategorize and exclude fields. Without its own exclude it inherits the top-level one. Ids from the other standard are reported as unknown. Headlines for C++ guidelines go in the same .noyce/rules/headlines.json, keyed by id ("Rule 8.2.2"). Deviations work as for MISRA C. C++-specific limitations: Templates are checked as written (the declared pattern), not per instantiation. A construct that only arises for a particular template argument is not reported. virtual / override / final (Rule 13.3.1) resolves base classes among the classes the translation unit sees. A base defined only outside the project gives no finding. Exceptions in the licensed text are not applied unless they are certain. Rule 8.2.2 exempts only casts to void, Rule 8.2.5 exempts nothing, and Rule 13.3.1 also reports overriding destructors without override. These rules may over-report until reviewed against the licensed copy. The program model builds no control-flow graph for C++ functions containing try/catch, throw or range-based for (no implemented C++ rule needs one). The C++ qualification corpus (qualification/corpus/misra-cpp-rules, engine id misra-cpp-rules) is Noyce's own, not the licensed MISRA C++ Example Suite. See qualification/known-problems/misra-cpp-rules.md.

Only part of MISRA C:2012 is implemented; directives are not checked. The count is in the page subtitle. Only 31 of 179 MISRA C++:2023 guidelines are implemented, with categories from one unconfirmed public listing (see MISRA C++:2023). The rule engine's results are not yet counted as A-5 evidence; coding-standard objectives read cppcheck. In the Findings tab a possible violation looks like a violation; only the Summary's Possible column separates them. No guideline text; headlines only from your own .noyce/rules/headlines.json. The qualification corpus is Noyce's own, not the licensed MISRA Example Suite. Known problems include Rule 11.7 not being detectable end to end (clang rejects the construct), and essential-type rules that need review against the licensed edition. See qualification/known-problems/misra-rules.md and Qualification kits. The MISRA tile in Quality Trend uses a separate scan, not the rule engine.

Flowgraph & Cross-Reference shows each function's control-flow graph, its metrics against your quality model, and where each symbol is defined, read, written and called. Everything here is computed from the program model and tagged Derived. Open it with Noyce Compliance: Open Flowgraph & Cross-Reference, from the Compliance hub, or with Open flowgraph on a Quality Trend hotspot.

Select Compute metrics. It rebuilds the program model, then computes metrics for every function, and writes .noyce/analysis/metrics.json. Until then the view reads "Not measured — build the program model". The header shows how many functions and translation units were measured, any parse errors, and the model and engine version. The function list can be searched, filtered to Violations, and sorted by Complexity or File order. It shows V(G), ev(G), nesting depth and the number of violations.

Metric How it is computed Cyclomatic complexity V(G) E − N + 2 over the function's control-flow graph, at least 1. Essential complexity ev(G) V(G) after repeatedly collapsing structured single-entry, single-exit subgraphs. Maximum nesting, statements From the syntax tree. Knots Pairs of jump arcs that cross, in source-line order. Halstead Operators and operands (n1, n2, N1, N2), length, vocabulary, volume, difficulty (n1/2 · N2/n2) and effort (difficulty × volume). Lines Physical, blank, code and comment lines; comment density = comment lines ÷ code lines. Fan-in, fan-out Distinct callers and callees; pointer calls and parameter count. Returns Return points.

Limits live in .noyce/quality-model.json, written with defaults from the HIS Source Code Metrics 1.3.1 recommended limits the first time metrics are computed: cyclomatic ≤ 10, essential ≤ 4, nesting ≤ 4, knots 0, statements ≤ 50, parameters ≤ 5, fan-out ≤ 7, fan-in ≤ 5, returns ≤ 1, comment density ≥ 0.2. Edit the file for your project. A value violates a limit only when it is strictly outside it. The Metrics section of a function lists its violations as Metric, Value, Limit.
The Control flow graph section draws the selected function: a diamond is a decision, a dashed curve is a back-edge, and dotted or muted blocks are unreachable. Select a block to open its source line.
For the selected function, Globals accessed by function lists each global with its reads and writes. Choose any symbol to see its Definitions, Declarations, Reads, Writes, Callers and Callees.

Capture Snapshot in Quality Trend now uses these derived metrics. If the model cannot be built, it falls back to the older text-based estimate, says so, and only on that fallback shows the maintainability proxy ("Proxy, not the SEI index"). On the derived path maintainability is not computed: "no validated maintainability formula".

Coverage is not drawn on the flowgraph yet; the legend says "Coverage overlay: not measured". Symbols are matched by name, so two static functions or globals with the same name in different files are conflated. Calls and accesses through unresolved pointers are excluded from the cross-reference (their count is shown). Comment lines are counted for each translation unit's main file only, not its headers. Per-level limits in the quality model (byDal) are not applied by the view, and Quality Trend's "over 10" complexity count uses a fixed limit of 10 rather than the quality model. Compute metrics cannot be cancelled from this view.

DO-178C Table A-7 asks for statement, decision and MC/DC coverage (objectives 5 to 7, depending on level) and, at Level A, for object code that is not traceable to source to be verified (objective 9). Noyce IDE measures coverage in three ways, and shows each with its environment so you can see what kind of credit it supports: Way Environment State in this release Host coverage with LLVM Host, with vendor SDK calls stubbed Works in the IDE and the CLI. Target coverage probes Target One flow in the IDE (Target verification) and the CLI (noyce verify --target): build instrumented, flash, run, collect. Tested against a fake device and real toolchains; not verified on hardware. Object-code branch coverage Simulator or target trace Disassembly and trace import work in the IDE; no real trace has been ingested yet.
Open MC/DC Coverage from its tile or Noyce Compliance: Open MC/DC Coverage. It has three tabs: Decisions, Measured coverage and Review uncovered.

clang, llvm-nm (or nm), llvm-profdata and llvm-cov, LLVM 18 or newer, so that clang accepts -fcoverage-mcdc. Noyce IDE checks this by compiling a test file. Override the tools with NOYCE_COV_CC, NOYCE_COV_NM, NOYCE_COV_PROFDATA and NOYCE_COV_COV. With only GCC and gcov, Measure module is disabled with "This toolchain cannot measure MC/DC", and no coverage is measured. No statement or branch figure is shown in place of MC/DC.

Write a test driver with a main() under tests/mcdc/ that exercises one source file, and name that file in a comment: // @coverage-source ../../src/my_module.c. Add // @coverage-extra-source <file> for other files to link and // @coverage-include <dir> for include directories. In Measured coverage, pick the Module; the Driver follows it. Select Measure module. The module is built with LLVM's coverage and MC/DC instrumentation, the driver runs, and the result is read back. A run is a background job you can Cancel, limited to five minutes by default. Each record shows its environment, tool, MC/DC form and status. Reread results reads the records again. Vendor headers and functions the module needs but the host does not have are generated as stubs that return 0. The record lists every stubbed symbol, because a branch decided by a stub was decided by the stub, not by your code. The record is marked Host, stubbed, and its caveat says DO-178C 6.4.1 requires the differences between this environment and the target to be analysed before it counts as verification credit. noyce cover --host runs every driver in tests/mcdc/ and writes .noyce/coverage/<driver>.json and the merged mcdc.json.

Both unique-cause and masking MC/DC are measured. Choose the form with the setting noyce.coverage.mcdcForm (unique-cause by default, or masking); it is recorded on every coverage record and must match what your PSAC and SVP state.

A re-run of the same driver, module, environment and tool replaces the previous record. Records of different drivers for the same module are combined by their condition vectors, so an independence pair split across two drivers counts. Different environments or tools are not combined in the dashboard figure: each module counts the newest environment's records. A record measured on a different version of the source is excluded and listed as stale; measure the module again. A module that has not been measured counts its obligations with no coverage, marked "a structural zero, not a result".

For coverage on the target with your own toolchain, the noyce-core engine can instrument the sources: a statement probe at each basic block, and decision and condition probes that keep short-circuit evaluation. Instrumented copies go to .noyce/cov/build/<config>/, with a small runtime (noyce_cov.c, no heap, no C library) and a probe map; your sources are never edited. A statement-only mode is available for small parts, and an RTT streaming mode. Collected counter RAM becomes .noyce/coverage/cov-probe-<config>-<host|target>.json, tagged Measured, and appears in Measured coverage with tool "Noyce probes" and its chip, probe and MC/DC form.

MC/DC Coverage → Measured and Unit tests → On target have a Target verification section. It reads "Not verified on hardware — connect a probe" until a probe has produced a record. Build instrumented image instruments the project's own C sources (vendor trees, SDK paths, system_*.c and SEGGER RTT are left out, with the reason), stages them as overlay slots and builds the firmware with the portable build and your cross toolchain. The image, its link map, the probe map and image.json (the image hash) go to .noyce/cov/build/target/. No probe is needed. Flash & run takes the image last built (refusing one whose hash changed, or built for other tests), attaches, flashes with read-back verification, runs, halts and reads the counters. Build, flash & collect does both in one go. With target tests in tests/target/ the image runs them to their END line over RTT, masks interrupts, and is halted; without, the application runs for 5 seconds and is halted. Generated unit drivers copied there from Unit tests are compiled in place of their unit, so each unit is linked once. Tick Coupling probes to build .noyce/cov/build/coupling/target.elf instead, the image Data & Control Coupling's Collect from target reads. The steps show live: Detect probe, Read build and chip, Instrument sources, Build instrumented image, Attach, Flash and verify, Run, Halt, Read counters, Detach, Write records. The first one that fails stops the run and is named; the probe is always released. The counters are only ever read from the target's RAM; before reading, the image on disk is hashed again and must still be the one flashed, and the collected record must name that image and build. The run record (.noyce/verification/target-verify/runs/<id>.json) carries the chip, probe and serial, image hash, toolchain, the RTT text's hash and the coverage totals; the target tests' verdicts also go to Test Explorer's Run on target records. The chip comes from the Chip field, else the CubeMX .ioc (Mcu.UserName, e.g. STM32G431VBTx), else the build's MCU. The same flow runs headless as noyce verify --target (CLI). Limitation The flow is built and tested against a fake device and with real cross-compiles, but it has not been run on hardware. Do not rely on target probe coverage until a first board run has produced a record. A TI CCS project (Canister, TM4C1294) has no GNU ld linker script, so the portable build cannot link an image and the flow stops at Read build and chip. noyce cover --target <probe> --config <id> (--dumps … | --elf …) still collects from an image you built, flashed and ran yourself.
Open Object Code Traceability (Noyce Compliance: Open Object Code Traceability). It has three tabs: Untraceable runs, Object branches and Execution targets.

Build the firmware with -g, choose the image, then select Capture disassembly. Noyce IDE runs arm-none-eabi-objdump (or llvm-objdump, or objdump) on the linked image and analyses it in the view; nothing outside the app is needed. It looks on PATH and in the Arm toolchain set in noyce.stm32.armToolchainPath or noyce.stm32.cubeIdePath. Results are written to .noyce/socta/. An image with no DWARF line table is "Not analysed". Untraceable runs lists object code no source line accounts for, each needing a justification. At Level A a justification by one person shows Not independent.

Object branches lists every conditional branch in the image, mapped to a source decision where there is one. A branch with no source decision (compiler-generated code such as switch tables or division helpers) must be covered or justified. Until a trace is imported the tab reads Not measured: branch outcomes are unknown, not zero. Run the image yourself, then select Import trace…. Accepted formats: QEMU -d exec,nochain log, or the QEMU execlog plugin output; Renode ExecutionTracer output (PC, PCAndOpcode or Disassembly; opcode-only is refused); an address list decoded from ETM or MTB trace, which must say which. ETM and MTB decoding is not done in Noyce IDE. The trace is copied to .noyce/objcov/traces/. A trace taken from a different build of the image is not joined.

Execution targets lists what can run the image here: hardware through probe-rs, QEMU and Renode, and whether each was found. Simulator support by part is taken from the simulators' documentation, marked Not verified: STM32G431 (the H-Bridge controller): no STM32G4 machine in QEMU, and no STM32G4 platform confirmed in Renode. Object coverage needs ETM trace from the target, if the part has it fitted, or a core-only QEMU board for portable code. TM4C1294 (the Canister controller): no Tiva C machine in QEMU (lm3s6965evb is a different part) and none confirmed in Renode. Use hardware trace. LimitationNo real execution trace has been ingested yet; only synthetic fixtures were tested, and a fixture trace is marked "it is a fixture and will not count as evidence". There is no button to run QEMU or Renode from the view, although the Not measured notice suggests running them: run the simulator yourself and import its trace.

The Review uncovered tab of MC/DC Coverage lists every obligation left uncovered by measured runs, and asks a person to classify each one: Classification Effect Missing test case Drafts a verification case for the requirement you name. The item stays open until a test covers it. Dead code Raises a problem report. The item stays open: dead code is removed, not justified away. Deactivated code Closes the item. Needs the mechanism (configuration or design), a reference, and how execution is prevented. Justified Closes the item, with the analysis. Signing. Choose who signs under Signed by, a person on the roster (an AI never counts). Closing classifications need the verifier role. At Levels A and B the signer must be independent of the code's authors, which are read from the file's git history. If the file has no git history, an Independent reviewer with the verifier or SQA role co-signs. Select Sign classification; the record is written to the audit trail. Records are append-only, one file each under .noyce/process/coverage-classifications/. A record stops counting, and shows Reclassify, when the source changed since it was signed, the record was altered, or the signer left the roster. Obligations that cannot be proven either way, for example a macro decision whose MC/DC LLVM did not report, show "Measure again before classifying" and cannot be classified. The review counts an obligation as covered if any record from the same tool covered it, in any environment; the dashboard figure counts only each module's newest environment. The two can therefore differ.

Host coverage needs LLVM/Clang 18 or newer; there is no gcov path. Host records are stubbed; DO-178C 6.4.1 environment analysis is yours to do. Target probe coverage is unverified on hardware; the flow has been tested against a fake device only. Object-code coverage has been tested with synthetic traces only. QEMU and Renode do not model STM32G431 or TM4C1294; ETM or MTB traces must be decoded outside Noyce IDE. Known engine problems are listed in qualification/known-problems/ (cov-host.md, cov-probe.md, object-coverage.md); for example, LLVM's summary reports 0/0 MC/DC for decisions inside macros although its detail is correct.

DO-178C A-7(8) asks that tests exercise the data and control coupling between components. Noyce IDE enumerates every coupling from the program model, measures which ones a requirements-based test run actually exercised, and lets a rostered person justify the rest. Open it with Noyce Compliance: Open Data & Control Coupling or the DC/CC analysis tile. What is a coupling. A data coupling is a writer in one component, a variable, and a reader in another. A control coupling is a call from one component into another, including calls through function pointers, whose candidate targets are the address-taken functions of a matching type.

Analyze coupling parses the project's own sources and enumerates every coupling between components. Vendor trees are out of scope. The result is written to .noyce/coupling/static.json. Measure coupling (host) builds each host test driver twice, plainly and with coupling probes, runs it case by case, and collects which couplings each test exercised. Drivers are tests/**/test_*.c files that carry the same @coverage-source comments as MC/DC drivers. Results go to .noyce/coupling/measured-*.json, and test results are appended to .noyce/verification/results.jsonl. Review the table. The default filter is Open; others are Not measurable, Satisfied and All. Both jobs run in the background with Cancel. Analyze is limited to 10 minutes, Measure to 20.

A coupling is Satisfied only when a test run exercised it and that run is requirements-based: a verification case in Evidence Records → Verification cases names the test, verifies at least one requirement, and its latest result is a pass with an execution record. Requirement ids are never guessed from test names. A coupling exercised only by other tests reads Not by a requirements test. A coupling no test exercised can be Justified: a reason, an author on the roster, and at Levels A and B a reviewer who is a different person on the roster. Justifications are stored in .noyce/coupling/justifications.json. Unresolved accesses (pointer accesses, escaped addresses and pointer calls the analysis could not resolve) are listed separately and must each be justified. The objective is satisfied only when nothing blocks it. What keeps A-7(8) open lists the blockers: not analyzed, not measured, couplings not exercised, couplings outside the measured build, no requirements-based runs, unjustified unresolved accesses, or a component map nobody has reviewed.

Which source files make up each component comes from the SDD's component table (columns Component and Source Files). Without one, each source file is its own component, and the view says this is a default, not the design. The map is stored in .noyce/coupling/components.json. Choose a reviewer on the roster and select Record review; editing the map afterwards makes the review stale. The map can only be edited by hand in that file.

The view uses the software level recorded in Compliance. If none is recorded it assumes Level A and shows "(assumed)". noyce couple refuses to assume a level. Limitation Collect from target (probe) reads .noyce/cov/build/coupling/target.elf. Build it with Coupling probes ticked in Target verification (or noyce verify --target --coupling), which also flashes, runs and collects in one go. Target coupling collection is unverified on hardware. A test driver whose instrumented run behaves differently from its plain run is dropped from the measurement without a notice in the view. The Compliance Dashboard and the life-cycle documents still use the older name-matching estimate when no measured report exists; that estimate is marked heuristic and cannot close A-7(8). Known engine problems, such as memcpy counting as a whole-object access and interrupt and thread probes not being serialised, are listed in qualification/known-problems/coupling.md.

Execution time and stack depth measured on the target, compared with the static worst-case stack. Open it with Noyce Compliance: Open Timing & Stack. Every measured figure is labelled "measured — not a bound": a measurement shows what happened in that run, never a worst case.

With unit drivers in tests/target/, noyce verify --target --timing does steps 1 to 4 in one go: one timing site per driver, the runtime compiled into the verification image, collected after coverage. Select Prepare runtime. It writes the timing runtime to .noyce/timing/build/<config>/. Add those sources to your build, compile with -DNOYCE_TIMING -DNOYCE_TIMING_HAS_CONFIG -I <dir>, and link with the -Wl,--wrap=… options the notice lists for interrupt handlers. Call noyce_timing_init() and noyce_stack_paint() first in main. Flash and run the firmware, attach the debug probe in the Debug Probe view, and halt the target. Select Collect from target. Results go to .noyce/timing/timing-<config>-target.json. Set Core clock to see microseconds; it is read from the project's CubeMX .ioc file when there is exactly one, otherwise type it. Without a clock, times stay in cycles. Config names the build. How it measures. Time uses the DWT cycle counter around each timed site. Cortex-M0, M0+ and M23 have no cycle counter, so time is Not measured there. Stack depth comes from painting the stack with a pattern and reading the high-water mark; painting needs CMSIS (__StackLimit / __StackTop) or STM32Cube (_estack, _Min_Stack_Size) symbols in the linker script. Interrupt handlers are timed only, not painted. Durations above 2^32 cycles wrap without detection. Per-call figures come from the unit test drivers built with -DNOYCE_TIMING. Static worst case walks the program model's call edges with the compiler's .su stack-usage files, so build with -fstack-usage and build the program model (Build program model). It reports main plus every handler nested at once; NVIC priorities would lower that. The walk does not follow function-pointer calls. WCET. Noyce IDE does not compute worst-case execution time. Import WCET report… reads bounds from an external analyser (noyce.wcet/1 JSON, or CSV with function and wcet_cycles or wcet_us columns) and compares measurements with them: "Within bound" is consistent, never a confirmation. Limitation On-target collection (cycle counter, stack painting, probe-rs reads) has not been verified on hardware. A static stack figure reads Complete even when the code calls through function pointers; those calls are listed only in the warnings and are not counted. The runtime wraps every handler the static walk recognises by name, including reset and fault handlers. Check the wrap list before you build.

Finds every interrupt service routine and every global accessed from both interrupt and thread context, and flags accesses that can be torn or lost. Open it with Noyce Compliance: Open Interrupt & Shared Data, or run it with noyce analyze. Results are Derived and stored in .noyce/analysis/concurrency/result.json. Analyze builds the program model, then analyses it; Re-run without rebuilding model skips the build. Interrupts are found from C vector-table initialisers, assembly vector tables, interrupt attributes and vendor keywords, and run-time registration calls such as IntRegister. A handler found only by its name is listed as unconfirmed and not analysed as an ISR. Thread context is main, the reset handler, and RTOS task entries (FreeRTOS xTaskCreate, CMSIS-RTOS osThreadNew, ThreadX tx_thread_create). Findings: non-atomic read-modify-write, multi-word access, a function that runs in both contexts, missing volatile, and unprotected write/write. Each is Definite or Possible, with the reason when it is only possible (for example protected on some paths only, or the interrupt was found only by registration). Accesses inside a recognised critical section (__disable_irq/__enable_irq, IntMasterDisable/Enable, BASEPRI and PRIMASK writes, FreeRTOS and CMSIS-RTOS critical sections, __HAL_LOCK), or made before interrupts are enabled, are listed as suppressed with what protected them. The results support DO-178C A-5(6); "Analysis, not a review; these results support A-5.6 and cannot satisfy it alone." Note All RTOS tasks are treated as one thread context, so task-against-task races are not reported, and nested interrupt priorities are not modelled, so interrupt-against-interrupt races are not reported. The critical-section, interrupt-enable and task-creation lists are built in; there is no project file to change them in this release. Pointer aliasing is not resolved; unresolved pointer accesses are listed for review. Functions reachable only through unresolved function pointers are in no context.

Target coupling collection is built and tested against a fake device only; it is unverified on hardware. Timing and stack collection on the target is unverified on hardware; no static WCET is computed. The interrupt analysis's configuration lists are not user-configurable.
Unit Tests builds a test driver for one function at a time from the program model, and keeps its test vectors in a table you edit. Open it with Noyce Test: Open Unit Tests.

If there is no model yet, select Build program model. Functions in vendor trees and functions defined in headers are not listed. Select a function. The view shows its signature, file, the globals it reads and writes, the callees it stubs, and whether register accesses use a register-file fake (from the SVD file, or an architectural address map). Review the Test vectors. Rows are proposed from the parameter types: boundary, equivalence and robustness values for fixed-width integers, bool, char and size_t. Other types get no proposed values. Fill each row's expected values. Enter your name in Engineer name first; the row records who filled it and when. Select Save row. Select Generate driver to write the driver, or Run on host to generate it, build it and run it. Expected values never come from running the code. Every proposed row starts with its expected values pending: "Pending rows can never pass. Expected values come from requirements or an engineer, never from running the code." A pending row is skipped in the host driver, left out of the target driver, and reads pending in the results. Inputs and expected values are JSON, for example {"param:x": 1} and {"return": 2}. Inputs can set param:, global:, stub:<callee>.returns (a sequence of returns) and reg:0x… keys; expected values can check return, outputs through pointers, globals, stub call counts and arguments, call order, and registers. Requirement ids link a row to the requirements it verifies.

Choose MC/DC or Branch and select Propose inputs (CBMC). CBMC searches for inputs that reach each coverage goal of the function, with the generated stubs, and adds the new inputs as rows (origin cbmc-mcdc or cbmc-branch) with expected values pending. Goals CBMC could not reach are listed; that is not a proof that they are unreachable. Inputs CBMC cannot set (structures, function pointers, nested pointers) are listed under Inputs not proposed. CBMC must be installed; see Formal Verification.

Run on host builds the driver with the generated Makefile (clang unless CC is set) using Unity, runs it, and records the run. Latest run shows pass, fail, pending and not run. Each run carries the note that host execution does not establish target compatibility, timing or peripheral behaviour (DO-178C 6.4.1). Regression compares the latest run with the previous run, or with the latest run tagged with the current document-set baseline, and lists rows that regressed, were fixed, are new or were removed. Flaky rows passed and failed with the same source and inputs. LimitationRuns are tagged with the document-set baseline by reading .noyce/set-baseline.json, but the baseline is stored at .noyce/documents/set-baseline.json. In this release runs are therefore never tagged, and comparing with Current set baseline finds no earlier run. Compare with Previous run.

Select Copy driver to tests/target to put the generated target_<unit>.c in tests/target/. Test Explorer's Run on target, and On target below the vectors (the target verification flow), then build it into the firmware test image: The driver is compiled in place of the unit's source, so the unit is linked once. It is self-contained: its stubs are inlined. Every symbol the driver defines on the unit's behalf (the stubs, their controls, test-owned globals) gets a name private to that file (noyce_t_<unit>__<name>), so the firmware's real collaborators and globals still link beside it. One driver per source file per image: two functions of the same file cannot be in tests/target/ together (the image would link that file twice). Keep one, run, then swap. A driver for a function in the file that defines main() cannot run on the target; the test image replaces that file. LimitationTarget unit runs are built, linked and checked against a fake device; they have not been run on hardware.

Path under .noyce/ Holds tests/<file>__<function>.vectors.json The vector table (schema noyce.unit-vectors/1). tests/build/<unit>/ The generated host driver test_<unit>.c, target driver target_<unit>.c, stubs, register-file fake, Makefile and CBMC harness. tests/unity/ The bundled Unity framework. tests/runs/<unit>/ One record per run, tagged Measured.

Target runs of generated drivers are unverified on hardware. Only one function's driver per source file can be in an image. The register-file fake stores values only; peripheral side effects and timing are not simulated. CBMC runs with the host architecture and a fixed unwind of 16, so its proposals are bounded. Structures passed by value, nested pointers and function pointers get no proposed inputs. Comparison with the document-set baseline does not work (see above). Firmware that needs Arm-only instructions or linker symbols does not build on the host.

Every objective in DO-178C Annex A applies, applies with independence, or does not apply, depending on the software level. Grading, the Compliance Run and the PSAC, SVP, SCMP, SQAP and SAS all read that table. Noyce IDE can take it from three places, in this order of precedence: Source Badge What it carries Plans A licensed table you imported Imported Applicability, independence, control category, section references and outputs, entered from your licensed copy. Can be issued. The built-in table, verified Built-in, verified Applicability and independence only. Can be issued; control categories read "Not entered". The built-in table, not verified Built-in, unverified Applicability and independence only. Stay draft. You see the source on the Compliance Dashboard header line Annex A table, with Verify… and Import licensed table… beside it, and in Evidence Records → Annex A table.

Noyce IDE ships a matrix of the 71 objective ids against levels A to E: applies with independence, applies, or not applicable. It contains no objective wording, outputs, control categories or section references; those are RTCA's licensed text and come only from an imported table. The matrix is the product author's transcription. Its totals match the widely cited DO-178C totals (applicable A 71, B 69, C 62, D 26, E 0; with independence A 30, B 18, C 5, D 2), but a matching total does not prove every cell. That is why it counts for your project only after two people have checked it against a licensed copy. Every built-in cell carries the provenance declared, producer noyce.builtin-annex-a. While the table is unverified, the Compliance Dashboard shows the notice Annex A from built-in table, not verified: "PSAC, SVP, SCMP, SQAP and SAS stay draft until two rostered people verify it, or a licensed table is imported." Those documents carry the note "Applicability from built-in table — not yet verified against a licensed copy", and an issued one says it is not for submission.

Two different people on the roster each confirm every cell against their own licensed copy. Add both to the roster first; with fewer than two people the panel says "The roster needs two people". Select Verify… on the Compliance Dashboard, or open Evidence Records → Annex A table. Choose yourself under Verifier and name your copy under Licensed copy (for example the RTCA document and licence number). Pick a table (A-1 to A-10). For each objective and level, the cell shows Built-in: and its value. Set what your copy says: Agree — … or Disagree — … with the value your copy gives. Cells marked check first are the ones the author is least sure of. Agree with the rest of A-n marks every cell you have not touched in that table as agreeing. Use it only after reading the table. When all 355 cells (71 objectives × 5 levels) are marked, select Sign verification. The table becomes Built-in, verified when: two distinct people on the roster have each signed a verification (an AI identity never counts), every value each of them stated equals the effective value of every cell, and neither record is stale. Each record carries the SHA-256 of the matrix it checked; if a product update or an override changes any cell, the record stops counting ("matrix changed since verification; verify again"). A person who verifies again replaces their own earlier record. Records are stored one file per record under .noyce/process/annex-a-verification/.

sections.h: Resolve a disagreement with an override
sections.t: A disagreement does not change the table by itself. Under Disagreements to resolve, each cell where a verifier's copy differs is listed as "name reads value; matrix has value". Choose who records the override under Override recorded by (a person on the roster). Under Reason, say what the licensed copy states and where. Select Override to value. The override is itself a signed record and changes the effective cell for this project. Because the matrix changed, any verifier who agreed with the old value has to verify again.

If your organisation holds the licensed DO-178C text, import the full table instead. Run Noyce Compliance: Import Licensed Annex A Table (applicability, independence), or select Import licensed table… on the Compliance Dashboard. Open blank template writes a template with the 71 objective ids and opens it. Fill every empty value from your licensed copy and save. Load filled template reads it into the form, or paste the table JSON. The form lists what is still missing: objectives, applicability or independence per level, section references, outputs or control categories. Enter Your name (a person, not an agent) and the Licensed copy, then select Import and sign. The table is stored in .noyce/compliance/annex-a-licensed.json with its content hash, and takes precedence over the built-in table. Verifying the built-in table changes nothing while an imported table stands.

The built-in table carries no control categories, section references or outputs; those read "Not entered — control categories come only from an imported licensed table" until a licensed table is imported. The built-in table has not been verified by Noyce against a licensed copy. Your project's two verifications are what make it usable. ISO 26262 and IEC 61508 have their own built-in method tables with the same verification rules; see ISO 26262 and IEC 61508. IEC 62304 has none.

ISO 26262-6 and IEC 61508-3 do not list objectives the way DO-178C Annex A does. They list methods and techniques, each with a recommendation per integrity level: ++ highly recommended, + recommended, o no recommendation (ISO 26262, per ASIL A–D); HR, R, - and NR not recommended (IEC 61508, per SIL 1–4). Noyce IDE grades a project against these tables with the same rules as Annex A: a built-in table that counts only after two people verify it, signed overrides, or a licensed table you import.

The Compliance Run grades the framework and level your project has recorded on the Compliance Dashboard. A recorded DO-178C software level takes precedence, so an existing DO-178C project is graded exactly as before. Otherwise the run uses the ISO 26262 ASIL or the IEC 61508 SIL you recorded. No level is assumed: with none recorded, Take a run asks you to choose one. ASIL QM levies no Part 6 method table, so a run at QM is refused with "ASIL QM levies no ISO 26262-6 method table".

Standard Tables built in Entries Cells Least certain Not entered ISO 26262-6:2018 6-1 to 6-12 79 316 88 4 (row 6-10.1d) IEC 61508-3:2010 A.1, A.3, A.4, A.5, A.9, B.1, B.2, B.3, B.8, B.9 78 312 88 0 The tables hold entry ids and recommendation symbols only. They contain no method names, no clause text and no table titles; the short topic shown beside each table id is Noyce's own label. Every cell carries the provenance declared (producer noyce.builtin-iso26262-6 or noyce.builtin-iec61508-3). Each entry records its source: ISO 26262-6 Table 6-1 rows 1a–1h and IEC 61508-3 Table B.9 match a public reproduction (exida, "Software Metrics: ISO 26262 / IEC 61508", 2018). Every other entry is the product author's transcription, not checked against a licensed copy. Cells the author is least sure of are marked check first in the verification checklist. A cell that could not be stated from public sources is Not entered rather than guessed: it is neither met nor missed, and it has to be filled by an override before the table can be verified. Tables not listed above (for example ISO 26262-6 Tables 13 onward, IEC 61508-3 Table A.2) are not built in; they come only from a licensed import. While the table is unverified, the Compliance Dashboard shows ISO 26262-6 method tables from built-in table, not verified (or the IEC 61508-3 equivalent): "Runs graded against it cannot be exported and plans stay draft until two rostered people verify it, or a licensed table is imported."

The checklist is the same as for Annex A. Two different people on the roster each confirm every cell against their own licensed copy. Select Verify… on the Compliance Dashboard, or open Evidence Records → ISO 26262-6 method tables (or IEC 61508-3 technique tables). The tab is named for the project's framework. Choose yourself under Verifier and name your copy under Licensed copy. Pick a table. For each entry and level, set what your copy says: Agree — …, Disagree — …, or, for a not-entered cell, State — … with the value your copy gives. Agree with the rest of table marks every untouched stated cell as agreeing. Not-entered cells are left for you to state. When every cell is marked, select Sign verification. The table becomes Built-in, verified when two distinct rostered people have signed, every value each stated equals the effective cell, no cell is still not entered, and neither record is stale. Each record carries the SHA-256 of the table it checked; an override or a product update re-opens it. Records are stored one file per record under .noyce/process/iso26262-6-verification/ or .noyce/process/iec61508-3-verification/, and are release inputs. Under Cells to resolve, a disagreement or a stated not-entered cell is turned into an override: choose Override recorded by, give a Reason, and select Override to value. The override is a signed record; both verifiers then verify the changed table again.

Open Import a licensed table instead at the bottom of the checklist. Write blank template writes .noyce/compliance/<standard>-licensed.template.json with every entry id and empty cells. Fill every cell (and, optionally, the method names) from your licensed copy, paste the JSON, choose Imported by and select Import and sign. The table is stored at .noyce/compliance/iso26262-6-licensed.json or .noyce/compliance/iec61508-3-licensed.json with its content hash, and takes precedence over the built-in table. A table edited after import no longer verifies and is ignored.

An ISO 26262 or IEC 61508 run shows Highly recommended methods as its headline figure and a method-table section in place of Annex A. Each entry reads its recommendation at your level, then: Evidenced: a producer that genuinely applies the method ran and passed. Failing: that producer ran and failed (for example a levied coverage criterion below 100%). Open: highly recommended or recommended, with no evidence. Many methods (walk-throughs, design notations, defensive implementation) have no producer in Noyce IDE; a review record or a justification closes them. Advisory: evidence exists but cannot close anything (heuristic, or declared without a rostered signer). Not levied: no recommendation at this level. Not entered: the table does not state the cell. Which producers evidence which entries: Producer ISO 26262-6 IEC 61508-3 MISRA C analysis 6-1.1b, 6-1.1c, 6-7.1h, 6-10.1g A.3.3, A.4.5, A.9.3, B.1.1 CodeQL 6-7.1h, 6-10.1g A.9.3 CBMC 6-7.1e A.5.10, B.8.9 Verification cases (executed) 6-7.1j, 6-8.1a A.5.4 Requirements trace — A.5.9 Structural coverage (measured) 6-9.1a statement, 6-9.1b branch, 6-9.1c MC/DC B.2.7b statement, B.2.7c branch, B.2.7d MC/DC Data and control coupling (measured) 6-10.1f, 6-12.1b A.5.7 Timing & Stack (measured record) 6-7.1m, 6-10.1d A.5.5 Measured timing is a resource-usage evaluation and performance test, never a WCET analysis. CBMC is bounded model checking, not a formal proof.

Only a criterion the table rates highly recommended at your level is levied, at 100%. A recommended criterion is measured and reported but never failed, because both standards let a justified alternative replace it. From the built-in tables: Level Statement Branch MC/DC ASIL A 100% levied recommended recommended ASIL B 100% levied 100% levied recommended ASIL C recommended 100% levied recommended ASIL D recommended 100% levied 100% levied SIL 1 recommended recommended recommended SIL 2 100% levied recommended recommended SIL 3 100% levied 100% levied recommended SIL 4 100% levied 100% levied 100% levied Overrides and an imported table change these thresholds. The run lists the wording for your level, for example "MC/DC: recommended at SIL 3 — measured and reported, not levied (a justified alternative may replace it)". A run graded against the unverified built-in table records that in its configuration and cannot be exported: "ISO 26262-6:2018 recommendations from the built-in table — not yet verified against a licensed copy."

The built-in tables have not been verified by Noyce against licensed copies; your project's two verifications are what make them usable. Only part of each standard's tables is built in (see the table above). IEC 62304 and EN 50716 have no built-in table. The plans and documents Noyce IDE generates are DO-178C documents; ISO 26262 and IEC 61508 work products are not generated. Most methods have no producer and stay open until a review or justification closes them outside the run.

When you take certification credit for a tool's output without verifying that output by other means, DO-178C §12.2 asks you to qualify the tool. Noyce IDE's verification engines, such as host coverage or the MISRA rule checker, are such tools. For each one, Noyce provides qualification data and assembles it into a signed kit for one exact engine version. ImportantA kit is qualification data, not a qualification. Its Tool Qualification Plan and Tool Accomplishment Summary are templates that only you, the applicant, can complete: certification basis, operational environment, credit sought and liaison. The criterion and TQL shown for each engine are Noyce's proposal; you confirm or replace them in your PSAC.

Engine id Engine Known problems file cov-host Host structural coverage (statement, decision, MC/DC) yes cov-probe Target structural coverage probes yes coupling Measured data and control coupling yes object-coverage Object-code coverage and source-to-object traceability yes timing-stack Worst-case stack usage and timing measurement none recorded metrics Code metrics and flowgraphs none recorded concurrency Concurrency and shared-data analysis yes unit-gen Unit test generation and execution yes misra-rules MISRA C rule checker yes Each is classified as §12.2 criterion 3 (a verification tool whose defect could fail to detect an error), which is TQL-5 at levels A to D. The rationale, and when another criterion would apply, is shown for each engine.

These files are in the Noyce IDE source repository, not in your project: Artefact Location Tool Operational Requirements (TOR), with @tor ids docs/qualification/<engine>/tor.md Oracle corpus: inputs with independently reasoned expected results qualification/corpus/<engine>/<case>/ (case.json, expected.json, README.md, sources) Known problems: investigated defects, their TOR, root cause and credit impact qualification/known-problems/<engine>.md Differential comparisons against a reference tool qualification/differential/ Results record of a corpus run .noyce/qualification/<engine>/<engine version>/results.json Built kits .noyce/qualification/kits/<engine>/<engine version>/ In-situ re-run kits .noyce/qualification/in-situ/<engine>/<engine version>/ The engine version is <git commit>[-dirty]+<digest of the engine's source files>, so a kit identifies exactly which code it qualifies.

From a Noyce IDE source checkout: TerminalCopynoyce qualify --engine cov-host # one engine noyce qualify --all # every engine with an adapter npm run qualification:run -- --engine <id> does the same. Each case runs in a fresh temporary copy. A TOR passes only when at least one case verifies it and all its cases pass; an untested TOR fails the run. The results record carries a SHA-256 digest of its content and, if you have a signing key, an Ed25519 signature (results.sig.json). The corpus runs use the same tools as the engines: for coverage, a clang with -fcoverage-mcdc, llvm-profdata, llvm-cov and nm; for the sidecar engines, the noyce-core binary. The runner needs Node 26.

You sign kits with your own Ed25519 key. Noyce IDE never generates one for you. Create it once: TerminalCopynoyce kit --init-key # or: npm run qualification:kit -- --init-key The private key goes to ~/.config/noyce/qualification-signing.key (mode 600; NOYCE_SIGNING_KEY chooses another path), and the public key to qualification/signing-keys/ in the checkout, where verification looks for trusted keys. Then build, verify and export: Command Does noyce kit --engine <id> or --all Builds and signs a kit from the latest results. noyce kit --engine <id> --allow-dirty Builds a kit from a run taken on uncommitted code, marked DRAFT on every page and in the manifest. noyce kit --verify <kit-dir> Checks every file against the signed manifest and the signature against the trusted keys. noyce kit --verify-results <results.json> Checks one results record and its signature. noyce kit --in-situ --engine <id> [--dest <dir>] Exports the in-situ re-run kit. noyce kit --status [--engine <id>] Readiness and kit state for each engine. --public-key <pem> adds a trusted key for either verify command. A kit is refused, never built with a caveat, when the latest run has a failing or erroring case, an untested TOR, was a partial run of selected cases, has an altered record or signature, or was produced by a different engine version, corpus or TOR set than the checkout building the kit. A run on uncommitted code is refused unless you pass --allow-dirty. A kit contains: 01-TOR, 02-TOVV (verification cases, procedures and results), 03-KNOWN-PROBLEMS, 04-TCI (Tool Configuration Index), 05-TQP-TEMPLATE and 06-TAS-TEMPLATE, each as Markdown and as a formal .docx; results/results.json with its signature, tci.json, the engine's corpus, kit.html, INDEX.md, the signer's public key, and manifest.json with manifest.sig.json covering every file.

The in-situ kit lets the applicant re-run the corpus in their own environment and sign their own results. Hand them the folder: Check out Noyce IDE at the commit the kit names and install its dependencies. Install the production toolchain. The tool overrides are the same as in development (NOYCE_COV_CC, NOYCE_COV_PROFDATA, NOYCE_COV, NOYCE_COV_NM, NOYCE_CORE_BIN, NOYCE_CBMC). Create their own key: node tools/insitu.mjs init-key. Run NOYCE_ROOT=/path/to/noyce ./run.sh. They get their own signed results record and a signed comparison.json / comparison.md: case-by-case and TOR-by-TOR agreement with the shipped results, and every toolchain or platform difference. Exit 0 means their run passed and agrees; 1 it failed or differs; 2 an environment problem. Agreement is evidence for their Tool Qualification Plan, not a qualification by itself.

Open Evidence Records → Tool qualification. Below the project's tool register, the kits table lists the nine engines with Criterion · TQL at the project's level, Latest run, Version and Kit. Select an engine for Build kit, Verify kit and Export in-situ kit. Every disabled button says why, and a refused kit lists the builder's reasons. LimitationThe kit actions run from a Noyce IDE source checkout and read that checkout's .noyce/qualification/, not your firmware project's. An installed app without the corpus says "Kit status not measured" and builds nothing. Run noyce qualify and noyce kit from the checkout root (or pass --out <checkout>/.noyce), or the panel will not see the results.

Kits are built only from a Noyce IDE source checkout; the installed app does not include the corpus or the kit builder. The corpus runner needs Node 26. timing-stack and metrics have no known-problems file; that means none is recorded, not that the engines are free of defects. The TQP and TAS are templates you complete.

title: Command line, CI and team use

sections.t: The noyce command runs the same services the IDE panels run, bundled for Node. A record the CLI writes is the record the IDE writes for the same action, so opening the project in the IDE shows the CLI's results.

The CLI ships in the Noyce IDE source repository as packages/noyce-engine. From a checkout: TerminalCopynpm ci npm run engine:build # bundles the engine for Node node packages/noyce-engine/bin/noyce.mjs --help # or: npx noyce --help, npm run noyce -- --help Commands that analyse code (model, analyze, cover, verify, couple, grade) need the noyce-core sidecar binary. The CLI looks for it in this order and never builds it: NOYCE_CORE_BIN, services/noyce-core/target/release/noyce-core, services/noyce-core/target/debug/noyce-core, then packages/noyce-engine/vendor/noyce-core. If none is found it exits 3 and lists what it tried.

Every command takes --project <path> (default: the current directory), --json (one JSON document on stdout, schema noyce.cli/1) and --out <dir> (where records go; default <project>/.noyce/). Command Does what the IDE does at Writes model Builds the program model. .noyce/analysis/model/ analyze [--timeout <s>] [--include-vendor] [--no-extras] [--no-codeql] MISRA Diagnostics → Scan: every installed analyzer plus the rule engine, then metrics and concurrency (skipped with --no-extras), then a CodeQL scan if CodeQL is installed (skipped with --no-codeql). .noyce/compliance/static-analysis.json, .noyce/analysis/{rules,metrics,concurrency}/, .noyce/codeql/ cover --host MC/DC Coverage: runs every tests/mcdc/*.c driver. .noyce/coverage/ cover --target <probe> --config <id> (--dumps <a.bin,b.bin> | --elf <f>) [--uninstrumented-elf <f>] [--chip <name>] Attaches to the probe through probe-rs and collects target coverage, from counter-RAM dumps you captured or, with only --elf, by halting the core and reading the counters. <probe> is a probe serial or identifier, or auto. Always detaches. Untested on hardware. .noyce/coverage/cov-probe-*.json verify --target [--probe <serial|auto>] [--chip <name>] [--coupling] [--timing] [--run tests|duration] [--timeout <s>] [--duration <s>] [--statement] [--gcc-path <dir>] [--build-only | --reuse-image] Target verification → Build, flash & collect: detects the probe, builds the coverage-instrumented image with the portable build and your cross toolchain, flashes it, runs tests/target to their END line (or the application for --duration), halts, reads the counters and records them. Stops at the first step that fails and names it. Exit 3 when there is no probe or the target will not attach, flash or halt; 2 when the project cannot be built into an image; 1 when target tests fail, a run does not finish, or the counters do not belong to the flashed image. Unverified on hardware. .noyce/cov/build/target/, .noyce/coverage/cov-probe-target-target.json, .noyce/verification/target-verify/, .noyce/verification/target/ couple [--level <A-E>] Data & Control Coupling: analyze, measure and evaluate A-7(8). .noyce/coupling/, .noyce/verification/ trace Exports the traceability matrix. .noyce/do178c/traceability-matrix-<time>.csv grade [--level <A-E>] Compliance Run → Take run. .noyce/compliance-runs/<run-id>/ gate [--baseline <run|path>] [--regressions-only] Compares the newest run with a baseline. CI only. nothing kit … Builds, signs and verifies qualification kits. <out>/qualification/kits/ qualify --engine <id> | --all Runs the qualification corpus. <out>/qualification/<engine>/ Exit codes. 0 OK; 1 a gate or check failed; 2 usage or environment error (unknown command or flag, missing project, no runs to gate on, no software level); 3 a required tool is unavailable (no sidecar, no probe, no analyzer could run). An unknown flag is always exit 2; the CLI never runs a default in place of a mistyped flag. The software level is never assumed. couple uses --level, else the level recorded in Compliance. grade uses the recorded level, and accepts --level only when no level is recorded or when it equals the recorded one. With neither, the command exits 2: "Choose and justify the project software level in Compliance (or pass --level) before taking a run. No level is assumed."

noyce gate fails (exit 1) on: regressions against the baseline: a claim that was satisfied and now is missing or failing, a producer that ran and now does not, or fewer objectives evidenced; integrity problems: the run record fails its content hash, archived producer evidence is missing or altered, or the release inputs changed during or since the run; readiness blockers: a producer ran and is unsatisfied, the working tree was dirty or unknown, no commit was recorded, or conformity-review items are open. With --regressions-only, readiness blockers are reported as notes and do not fail the gate; regressions and integrity problems still do. Use it while a project is not yet certifiable, to gate on "nothing got worse". The baseline is --baseline (a run id, or a path to a run directory or its run.json), else the run marked as baseline (Mark as reference run in Compliance Run), else the run before the newest. TerminalCopy$ noyce grade --project fw --level C $ noyce gate --project fw --baseline run-20261103-170210 --regressions-only

sections.h: What the CLI does not do
sections.t: Target coverage collection is untested on hardware. Anything that needs a person (dialogs, AI agents, document authoring, signing a review) is refused with a reason.

templates/ci/ in the source repository holds a pipeline script and templates for GitHub Actions and GitLab CI: File Copy to, in your firmware project templates/ci/noyce-ci.sh .noyce/tools/noyce-ci.sh templates/ci/github/noyce-compliance.yml .github/workflows/ templates/ci/github/noyce-target-coverage.yml .github/workflows/ (self-hosted runner with a probe) templates/ci/gitlab/noyce-compliance.gitlab-ci.yml include it from .gitlab-ci.yml noyce-ci.sh looks for clang, llvm-cov, arm-none-eabi-gcc, cppcheck and cbmc and records what it found in toolchains.json, then runs model, analyze, cover, couple, grade and gate --baseline. It writes each step's JSON and log, summary.md and junit.xml to .noyce/tmp/ci/, and copies the graded run there for upload. Variable Default Meaning NOYCE noyce How to run the CLI, for example node /opt/noyce/packages/noyce-engine/bin/noyce.mjs. NOYCE_PROJECT . Project root. NOYCE_BASELINE content of .noyce/ci-baseline Baseline run id or path. Required. NOYCE_COVER host host or target. NOYCE_PROBE none Probe selector for target mode. With only this set, the step is noyce verify --target --probe <sel>: build, flash, run, collect. NOYCE_GCC_PATH none Cross toolchain bin directory for the instrumented build (optional). NOYCE_VERIFY_COUPLING, NOYCE_VERIFY_TIMING none 1 adds --coupling / --timing (optional). NOYCE_COVER_CONFIG none Collect-only: the instrumented build id; required with dumps or an ELF. NOYCE_COVER_DUMPS none Collect-only: comma-separated counter-RAM dumps from a run done outside the job. NOYCE_COVER_ELF none Collect-only: instrumented ELF; without dumps the CLI reads the counters live. NOYCE_COVER_UNINSTRUMENTED_ELF none Plain build, to measure probe overhead (optional). NOYCE_CHIP none probe-rs chip name when it cannot be auto-detected (optional). NOYCE_REQUIRED_TOOLS none Tools whose absence fails the job before any step runs. NOYCE_CI_OUT .noyce/tmp/ci Where outputs go. NOYCE_CI_LLVM_DIRS Homebrew LLVM prefixes Extra directories searched for LLVM tools. The job's exit code follows the CLI: 1 means a regression against the baseline; 2 a setup problem (no baseline, CLI not runnable, a target run with no probe); 3 a missing tool. A regression wins over an environment problem, and the environment annotations stay in the log. Baseline. Commit the run you accept under .noyce/compliance-runs/<run>/ and write its id to .noyce/ci-baseline. Re-baselining is then a reviewable commit. Signing. The pipeline never signs anything and never passes a key to the CLI. If NOYCE_SIGNING_KEY or NOYCE_QUALIFICATION_KEY is set in the job, it warns and still does not use it. LimitationWith NOYCE_COVER=target and no NOYCE_PROBE, the step stops with exit 2. In collect-only mode (NOYCE_COVER_DUMPS or NOYCE_COVER_ELF set) a missing NOYCE_COVER_CONFIG stops it with exit 2 and an annotation naming what is missing; cover is not run. A runner with no probe plugged in makes verify exit 3 (tool unavailable), never a regression.

A team shares .noyce/ through git, like the code. No server is involved. One file per record. These stores keep each record in its own file, so two people adding records on two branches never conflict: Store Directory under .noyce/ Review records process/reviews/ Problem reports process/problem-reports/ MISRA deviations process/deviations/ Roster process/roster/ Coverage classifications process/coverage-classifications/ Annex A verifications and overrides process/annex-a-verification/ Trace links and their suspect-link reviews requirements/trace-links/ Adding a record adds a file. Editing a record rewrites only its file, so two branches conflict only when they make different decisions on the same record, which a person should resolve. Append-only records (reviews, coverage classifications) are named by id plus a digest of their content, and are never rewritten. Removing an editable record writes a tombstone instead of deleting the file. An older single-file store (process/review-records.jsonl and the like) is still read, and is split into one file per record the first time the IDE writes to it. Upgrade the whole team together: an older IDE build still writes the old single file. The audit ledger is one hash chain, so it merges with a git merge driver instead. Set it up once per project, then once per clone: TerminalCopybash <noyce>/templates/team/install-team-git.sh # once per project; commit the results git config merge.noyce-ledger.name "Noyce audit ledger merge" git config merge.noyce-ledger.driver "node .noyce/tools/noyce-ledger-merge.mjs %O %A %B %P" The driver verifies both sides and refuses to merge a ledger that does not verify. It keeps every entry from both sides, orders new entries by time, re-chains them after the shared prefix and appends a ledger.merged entry recording each moved entry's old and new position, so an old signature citation still resolves. What to commit. Everything under .noyce/ except caches and scratch. The IDE writes .noyce/.gitignore listing build trees (build/, cov/build/, tests/build/, timing/build/), the program model (analysis/model/), tmp/, CodeQL databases, the search index and downloaded manuals. Never ignore the whole of .noyce/: that hides the evidence from configuration control.

These instructions run the CLI from a Noyce IDE source checkout; kit and qualify need one, because the corpora and kit builder live there. Target verification in CI needs a self-hosted runner with a probe and the cross toolchain, and is unverified on hardware. A central record server is not part of Noyce IDE; teams share records through git.

Noyce IDE never writes generated files into your source tree. Everything it produces for a project (analysis results, documents, evidence, the audit trail, agent state) goes into a .noyce/ folder at the project root.

Commit the life-cycle data in .noyce/ with the project: documents, requirements, review and verification records, compliance runs, change sets, configuration, and the audit ledger. The IDE does not commit these files for you. The IDE writes .noyce/.gitignore when .noyce/ is first created and checks for it when a workspace folder opens. It ignores only these regenerable caches and scratch files: gitignoreCopy/build/ /codeql/db-* /codeql/result-* /codeql/mirror-* /rag/ /manuals/ /knowledge/ /serial/ /architecture/model-cache.json /audit-ledger.json.tmp.* Downloaded vendor manuals can be downloaded again. The knowledge index, register code links, and graph are regenerated from the manual and project sources. Kept CodeQL evidence (codeql/last-scan-*.sarif) remains committable. The IDE replaces its legacy .gitignore header followed by a single *, but preserves user-edited ignore files. It also removes the legacy .noyce/ entry it wrote to .git/info/exclude; only .codegraph/ is excluded there. Other project or global ignore rules may still prevent files from appearing in Source Control.

Delete What happens rag/, architecture/model-cache.json, knowledge/ Rebuilt the next time you use the view. Re-indexing a manual or the workspace takes a few minutes. compliance/evidence-snapshot.json Rebuilt by the next dashboard scan. documents/, process/, audit-ledger.json, compliance-runs/ Lost for good. These are your records: issued documents, human reviews and the audit trail. Deleting the whole folder returns the project to a fresh state. Your source files are unaffected.
